This year's Nobel Prize in Physics rewards a telescope buried in Antarctic ice.
Every second, billions of ghost particles called neutrinos pass through your fingernail.
They fly straight through planets and people, almost never touching a single atom.
In 1988, physicist Francis Halzen had a wild idea: catch them with the ice at the South Pole.
IceCube froze 5,160 light sensors into a cubic kilometre of ice, down to 2,450 metres deep.
When a neutrino finally hits an atom, it makes a faint blue flash, and the sensors trace its path.
Neutrinos carry no charge, so magnetic fields can't bend them. They point straight back to their source.
That's how IceCube caught high-energy neutrinos from far beyond our solar system.
Halzen admits very few people thought it would work, including himself.
